# What p-values are not

<style>
  :root {
    --qr:           `r qr_css`;
    --lecture:      `r lecture_label`;
  }
</style>

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` slow lorises are the only known [venomous primates]{.hl}. Glands on the inside of their elbows make a secretion that turns venomous when mixed with saliva.

_Source: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance_
:::

## Today

The key points of three chapters of Winter (2019):

| Chapter | Topics |
|:--|:--|
| 10 | what p-values are not; power; Type I, II, M and S errors; multiple testing; stopping rules |
| 11 | confidence intervals, testing predictors with several levels, plotting uncertainty |
| 16 | strategies for model building, reproducible research |

. . .

Most of today is simulation: we make up a world where we know the truth, and see how our methods behave in it.

## So far

Lecture 9 introduced p-values, standard errors and confidence intervals, and showed that significance says nothing about size. Lectures 10 to 12 added mixed models with `lmer()` and `glmer()`, tested with likelihood ratio tests.

. . .

Today: how p-values can mislead, and how to plan and report models more carefully.

## Common misreadings

Lecture 9 listed what a p-value is not. For a p-value of .03, it does not mean:

- that there is a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true
- that there is a 97% chance that the effect is real
- that the effect is large or important

. . .

It means: if the null hypothesis were true, data at least this extreme would turn up 3% of the time.

## Absence of evidence

p > .05 does not mean that there is no effect.

. . .

The data are compatible with no effect, and they may be just as compatible with a large one, so look at the confidence interval. A small study can also miss a real effect, which is a question of power, coming next.

## Significant vs not significant {.smaller}

Two studies of the same effect (Gelman & Stern, 2006):

| | Estimate | SE | p | |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|:--|
| Study A | 25 | 10 | .01 | significant |
| Study B | 10 | 10 | .32 | not significant |

. . .

Do the two studies disagree? Test the difference:

```{r}
diff    <- 25 - 10
se_diff <- sqrt(10^2 + 10^2)
2 * pnorm(-diff / se_diff)
```

. . .

The difference between them is not significant either. To compare two studies, compare their effects directly.

# Power and errors

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` a threatened slow loris clasps its arms over its head. With its face markings, the pose looks like the hood of an angry [cobra]{.hl}.

_Source: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance_
:::

## Two ways to be wrong

|                      | No effect in reality       | Effect in reality         |
|----------------------|----------------------------|---------------------------|
| __Significant__      | Type I error (false alarm) | correct                 |
| __Not significant__  | correct                    | Type II error (miss)    |

. . .

We choose the Type I error rate, `α`, and usually set it to .05. [Power]{.hl} is the probability of finding an effect that is really there, 1 minus the Type II error rate. It grows with the effect size and the sample size, and shrinks as the noise grows.

## Simulating a study {.smaller}

A world we control: group b's vowels are 10 ms longer than group a's, SD = 40 ms.

```{r}
sim_study <- function(n, diff = 10, sd = 40) {
  d <- tibble(group    = rep(c("a", "b"), each = n),
              duration = rnorm(2 * n, mean = 200 + diff * (group == "b"), sd = sd))
  fit <- summary(lm(duration ~ group, data = d))$coefficients
  tibble(estimate = fit[2, 1], p = fit[2, 4])
}

set.seed(42)
one <- sim_study(n = 20)
one
```

. . .

The true difference is +10 ms. This study, with 20 speakers per group, estimates `r round(one$estimate, 1)` ms (p = `r round(one$p, 2)`): one study can be far off.

## Run it 1,000 times

```{r}
set.seed(42)
sims20 <- map(1:1000, \(i) sim_study(n = 20)) |> list_rbind()
mean(sims20$p < .05)
```

. . .

The power is about `r round(100 * mean(sims20$p < .05))`%: the effect is real, yet almost 9 studies in 10 miss it. A formula gives the same answer:

. . .

```{r}
power.t.test(n = 20, delta = 10, sd = 40)$power
```

## Power and sample size

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
set.seed(42)
pw <- tibble(n = c(20, 50, 100, 200, 300, 400)) |>
  mutate(power = map_dbl(n, \(k) mean(map_dbl(1:500, \(i) sim_study(n = k)$p) < .05)))

ggplot(pw, aes(n, power)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.8, colour = moss, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(colour = hornbill, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(colour = hornbill, size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 20, y = 0.85, label = "80% power", colour = mist, hjust = 0, size = 5.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Speakers per group", y = "Power")
```

For 80% power, this 10 ms effect needs about `r ceiling(power.t.test(power = 0.8, delta = 10, sd = 40)$n)` speakers per group. Plan the sample size before collecting data.

## Type M and Type S errors

Gelman & Carlin (2014) showed that with low power, significant results tend to be misleading.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
sims20 |>
  mutate(result = if_else(p < .05, "significant", "not significant")) |>
  ggplot(aes(estimate, fill = result)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2.5, boundary = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 10, colour = mist, linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 11.5, y = 85, label = "truth: 10 ms", colour = mist, hjust = 0, size = 5.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`not significant` = vine, significant = hornbill)) +
  labs(x = "Estimated difference (ms)", y = "Studies", fill = NULL)
```

Only the large estimates reach significance.

## Type M and Type S errors

```{r}
sig <- filter(sims20, p < .05)
mean(abs(sig$estimate))
mean(sig$estimate < 0)
```

. . .

The true difference is 10 ms. The significant estimates are on average `r round(mean(abs(sig$estimate)) / 10, 1)` times too large, a [Type M]{.hl} (magnitude) error, and `r round(100 * mean(sig$estimate < 0), 1)`% of them point the wrong way, a [Type S]{.hl} (sign) error. So a significant result from a small study probably exaggerates the effect.

## Power for mixed models

For mixed models, there is no simple formula. Do what we just did:

1. Simulate data with your design: participants, items, plausible effect sizes and random effects (lectures 10 to 12)
2. Fit the model to each simulated data set
3. Count how often the effect is significant

. . .

The `{simr}` package automates this for `lmer()` and `glmer()` models (Green & MacLeod, 2016).

## A pilot study {.smaller}

`naming_pilot` from {simling} is a pilot for this workflow: 15 younger and 15 older adults name the same 40 pictures. Is the frequency effect larger for older adults? Fit the model to the pilot, then let `{simr}` simulate larger studies from it:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(lme4)
library(simr)
pilot_data <- naming_pilot |> mutate(log_latency = log(latency))
pilot <- lmer(log_latency ~ age_group * freq_c + (1 + freq_c | participant) + (1 | picture),
              data = pilot_data)
bigger <- extend(pilot, along = "participant", n = 60)
powerSim(bigger, test = fixed("age_groupolder:freq_c", "lr"), nsim = 200)
```

. . .

The effect sizes in a pilot are themselves uncertain estimates. Check how the power changes with smaller, still plausible effects before you decide on a sample size.

# Multiple tests and stopping rules

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` slow lorises also use their venom on each other: in one study, 57% of males and nearly a third of females showed signs of at least one [venomous bite]{.hl}.

_Sources: Nekaris et al. (2020), Current Biology; Mongabay_
:::

## Multiple testing

Each test on a null effect has a 5% chance of a false alarm. With `k` tests:

```{r}
tibble(k = c(1, 5, 10, 20)) |>
  mutate(at_least_one_false_alarm = 1 - 0.95^k)
```

. . .

If you test 20 effects that do not exist, you will probably find at least one "significant" result.

## A simulation

1,000 studies, each running 10 t-tests on pure noise:

```{r}
set.seed(3)
any_sig <- map_lgl(1:1000, \(i) {
  p <- map_dbl(1:10, \(j) t.test(rnorm(20), rnorm(20))$p.value)
  any(p < .05)
})
mean(any_sig)
```

. . .

About `r round(100 * mean(any_sig))`% of the studies find "something".

## Correcting for multiple tests

```{r}
p <- c(0.003, 0.012, 0.031, 0.048, 0.21)
p.adjust(p, method = "bonferroni")
p.adjust(p, method = "holm")
```

Bonferroni multiplies each p-value by the number of tests; Holm does something similar, step by step, and loses less power.

. . .

Testing fewer things is even better. Decide which comparisons answer your question before you look at the data.

## Stopping rules

A tempting plan: test after every 10 participants, and stop as soon as p < .05.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.2
set.seed(8)
paths <- map(1:20, \(s) {
  a <- rnorm(100); b <- rnorm(100)
  tibble(study = s, n = seq(10, 100, by = 10),
         p = map_dbl(n, \(k) t.test(a[1:k], b[1:k])$p.value))
}) |> list_rbind() |>
  mutate(ever = any(p < .05), .by = study)

ggplot(paths, aes(n, p, group = study, colour = ever)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, colour = mist, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = vine, `TRUE` = hornbill),
                      labels = c("never below .05", "below .05 at some point")) +
  labs(x = "Participants per group so far", y = "p-value", colour = NULL)
```

20 studies of no effect: p-values wander, and some dip below .05 by chance.

## Peeking inflates false alarms

```{r}
peek <- function(max_n = 100, step = 10) {
  a <- rnorm(max_n); b <- rnorm(max_n)
  p <- map_dbl(seq(step, max_n, by = step), \(k) t.test(a[1:k], b[1:k])$p.value)
  any(p < .05)
}
set.seed(5)
false_alarm <- mean(map_lgl(1:1000, \(i) peek()))
false_alarm
```

Both groups come from the same distribution, and `peek()` returns `TRUE` if any of the 10 tests was below .05.

. . .

With 10 peeks, the false alarm rate is about `r round(100 * false_alarm)`%, not 5%. Fix the sample size in advance, and report how you chose it.

## Discussion

After 20 participants, your result is p = .07. Your supervisor suggests testing 10 more and checking again.

- What is the problem with this plan?
- What could you do instead, and how would you report what happened honestly?

# Uncertainty of regression estimates

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` in cool months, pygmy slow lorises can go into [torpor]{.hl}, a short form of hibernation. One study recorded inactivity lasting up to 63 hours.

_Source: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance_
:::

## Confidence intervals for coefficients

```{r}
words <- megastudy |> slice_head(n = 400)
m <- lm(rt ~ aoa, data = words)
coef(summary(m))
confint(m)
```

. . .

The first 400 words of `megastudy` (lecture 6). Each year of age of acquisition goes with about `r round(coef(m)[2])` ms more, and the 95% CI runs from `r round(confint(m)[2, 1], 1)` to `r round(confint(m)[2, 2], 1)` ms: roughly the estimate ± 2 SE.

## Predictors with several levels

```{r}
m_sp <- lm(duration ~ style, data = speech_styles)
coef(summary(m_sp))
```

. . .

Vowel duration in three speaking styles, from lecture 7: two coefficients, two treatment contrasts against casual speech. But is `style` as a whole a useful predictor?

## Testing the whole predictor {.smaller}

Compare models with and without it, as in lectures 11 and 12:

```{r}
m_0 <- lm(duration ~ 1, data = speech_styles)
anova(m_0, m_sp)
```

. . .

For `lm()`, the comparison is an [F-test]{.hl}; for `lmer()` and `glmer()`, a likelihood ratio test. Same idea: does the predictor improve the model?

## Showing uncertainty: categories

```{r}
new_sp <- tibble(style = levels(speech_styles$style))
preds  <- bind_cols(new_sp, predict(m_sp, newdata = new_sp, interval = "confidence"))
preds
```

. . .

`interval = "confidence"` adds the lower (`lwr`) and upper (`upr`) limits of the 95% CI.

## Showing uncertainty: categories

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.9
ggplot(preds, aes(style, fit)) +
  geom_jitter(data = speech_styles, aes(y = duration), width = 0.15,
              colour = kingfisher, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), width = 0.15,
                colour = hornbill, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(colour = hornbill, size = 4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Vowel duration (ms)")
```

## Showing uncertainty: continuous

Predict over a grid of ages of acquisition, within the range of the data:

```{r}
grid <- tibble(aoa = seq(min(words$aoa), max(words$aoa), length.out = 50))
grid <- bind_cols(grid, predict(m, newdata = grid, interval = "confidence"))
grid
```

## Showing uncertainty: continuous

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.2
ggplot(grid, aes(aoa, fit)) +
  geom_point(data = words, aes(y = rt), colour = kingfisher, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), fill = hornbill, alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(colour = hornbill, linewidth = 1.3) +
  labs(x = "Age of acquisition (years)", y = "Reaction time (ms)")
```

The band shows the uncertainty in the line, which is wider at the edges. `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` draws the same.

# Building models

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` the illegal [pet trade]{.hl} is one of the worst threats to slow lorises. Traffickers pull out their teeth so that they cannot bite.

_Sources: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance; Mongabay_
:::

## What you have learned

```{r}
#| echo: false
tibble(
  Outcome = c("continuous", "continuous", "binary (0/1)", "binary (0/1)"),
  `Repeated measures?` = c("no", "yes", "no", "yes"),
  Model = c("lm()", "lmer()", "glm(family = binomial)", "glmer(family = binomial)")
) |> knitr::kable()
```

. . .

We fitted `glmer()` in lecture 12, and `glm()` in tutorial 12 is the same model without random effects. All of them share one framework: an outcome, a linear predictor (continuous and categorical predictors, interactions), a distribution, and random effects where the data are grouped. Counts would use Poisson regression (Winter, Ch 13).

## The cookbook approach

Many textbooks teach a cookbook: two groups → t-test; three groups → ANOVA; two numbers → correlation.

. . .

Each of these tests is a special case of the [linear model]{.hl}; lecture 9 showed this for the t-test. The cookbook hides the assumptions behind each recipe, and it has no recipe once the data have repeated measures or several predictors. Winter recommends thinking in terms of models instead.

## Stepwise regression {.smaller}

Put in every predictor, and let the computer drop the useless ones:

```{r}
one_step <- function() {
  noise <- as_tibble(matrix(rnorm(50 * 21), ncol = 21,
                            dimnames = list(NULL, c("y", paste0("x", 1:20)))))
  best <- step(lm(y ~ ., data = noise), trace = 0)
  p <- summary(best)$coefficients[-1, 4]
  sum(p < .05)
}
```

. . .

The data have 50 rows: an outcome `y` and 20 predictors, all random noise. `y ~ .` uses every other column as a predictor, and `step()` drops predictors one at a time, as long as that improves the AIC.

## Stepwise regression finds noise

```{r}
set.seed(11)
n_sig <- map_dbl(1:300, \(i) one_step())
mean(n_sig >= 1)
```

. . .

In `r round(100 * mean(n_sig >= 1))`% of the data sets, the final model keeps at least one "significant" predictor, though nothing is real. Its p-values ignore all the tests that went into choosing it, a hidden case of [multiple testing]{.hl}. Choose predictors from your research question and theory instead.

## Theory-driven modelling

Winter (Ch 16): modelling is subjective, and that is fine, as long as it is principled and transparent.

- Decide the model before seeing the data: outcome, predictors, interactions, random effects
- Keep [confirmatory]{.hl} (planned) and [exploratory]{.hl} (after the fact) analyses apart, and label them
- Consider [preregistering]{.hl} the analysis
- Report the choices you made, and why

## Reproducible research

Someone else, or you in a year, should get the same results from your data.

| Practice | Instead of |
|:--|:--|
| the whole analysis as code, e.g. in R Markdown | clicking and copying results by hand |
| `set.seed()` before simulations or `sample()` | different random numbers on every run |
| R projects and relative paths | `C:/Users/me/Desktop/...` |
| `sessionInfo()` to record package versions | guessing which version gave the result |
| data and code shared with the paper, e.g. on the OSF | "available on request" |

# Your turn

## Exercises

1. Use `sim_study()` to estimate the power to detect a 20 ms difference (SD = 40) with 20 and with 50 speakers per group. Check your answers with `power.t.test()`
2. A study reports these p-values for 6 tests: 0.001, 0.008, 0.02, 0.04, 0.045, 0.3. Which remain below .05 after a Holm correction?
3. Fit `percent_v ~ language` on `rhythm_metrics`. Test `language` with a model comparison, and plot the predicted means with their 95% CIs

## Solutions {.smaller}

```{r}
set.seed(1)
mean(map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) sim_study(n = 20, diff = 20)$p) < .05)
mean(map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) sim_study(n = 50, diff = 20)$p) < .05)
power.t.test(n = c(20, 50), delta = 20, sd = 40)$power
```

. . .

Doubling the effect makes a huge difference: with 50 speakers per group, power is about `r round(100 * power.t.test(n = 50, delta = 20, sd = 40)$power)`%.

## Solutions {.smaller}

```{r}
p_ex <- c(0.001, 0.008, 0.02, 0.04, 0.045, 0.3)
p.adjust(p_ex, method = "holm")
```

. . .

Only the first two (`r paste(round(p.adjust(p_ex, method = "holm")[1:2], 3), collapse = " and ")`) stay below .05.

## Solutions {.smaller}

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.9
m_pv <- lm(percent_v ~ language, data = rhythm_metrics)
anova(lm(percent_v ~ 1, data = rhythm_metrics), m_pv)$`Pr(>F)`[2]

new_lang <- tibble(language = levels(rhythm_metrics$language))
preds_pv <- bind_cols(new_lang, predict(m_pv, newdata = new_lang, interval = "confidence"))
ggplot(preds_pv, aes(language, fit)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), width = 0.15, colour = hornbill, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(colour = hornbill, size = 4) + labs(x = NULL, y = "%V")
```

## Summary

::: {.takeaway}
- A p-value is not the probability that the null is true, and p > .05 does not show that there is no effect. Compare effects directly
- Low [power]{.hl} misses real effects, and exaggerates the ones it finds (Type M and S errors)
- Simulate to find out the power of a design, including mixed models
- Many tests and peeking at the data inflate false alarms: plan in advance
- Report [confidence intervals]{.hl}, and plot uncertainty
- Build models from theory instead of stepwise selection; keep your analysis [reproducible]{.hl}
:::

## References {.smaller}

- Gelman, A., & Carlin, J. (2014). Beyond power calculations: Assessing Type S (sign) and Type M (magnitude) errors. _Perspectives on Psychological Science_, 9(6), 641–651. https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691614551642
- Gelman, A., & Stern, H. (2006). The difference between "significant" and "not significant" is not itself statistically significant. _The American Statistician_, 60, 328–331. https://doi.org/10.1198/000313006X152649
- Green, P., & MacLeod, C. J. (2016). SIMR: An R package for power analysis of generalized linear mixed models by simulation. _Methods in Ecology and Evolution_. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12504
- Winter, B. (2019). _Statistics for linguists: An introduction using R_. Routledge.
